title: Heterogeneous treatment effects by firm size in DID

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with two-way fixed effects and an interaction that captures the extra tax reduction enjoyed by large firms.  

Treatment definition: `treated = 1` for large firms, `0` for small firms.  
Policy timing: `post = 1` from period 4 onwards for everybody (corporate-tax reform year).  
Causal parameter of interest: the coefficient on `treated × post`, i.e. the additional change in log-investment for large (vs. small) firms after the reform.  

Key identifying assumption (Parallel Trends): In the absence of the reform, the time trend in investment for large and small firms would have evolved in parallel. We probe this with a lead/lag (event-study) specification and with a placebo (“fake” reform in period 3).  

## 2. R Code
```r
############################################
#  Heterogeneous DID: Large vs. Small Firms
############################################
# Required packages
library(fixest)    # fast high-dim FE estimators
library(dplyr)     # data wrangling
library(readr)     # fast csv read

# 1. Read data -------------------------------------------------------------
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s09_data.csv"
df   <- read_csv(path,
                 col_types = cols(
                   unit_id      = col_integer(),
                   period       = col_integer(),
                   treated      = col_integer(),
                   post         = col_integer(),
                   treat_x_post = col_integer(),
                   y            = col_double()
                 ))

# 2. Baseline DID with two-way FEs ----------------------------------------
did_baseline <- feols(
  y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period,
  data     = df,
  cluster  = ~unit_id          # cluster at firm level
)

cat("\n=== Baseline DID ===\n")
print(coeftable(did_baseline)["treat_x_post", , drop = FALSE])

# 3. Robustness check 1: Event-study (leads & lags) ------------------------
# Adoption year = 4 for treated units, 0 (= never) for controls
df <- df %>% mutate(adopt_year = ifelse(treated == 1, 4, 0))

es <- feols(
  y ~ sunab(adopt_year, period) | unit_id + period,
  data    = df,
  cluster = ~unit_id
)

cat("\n=== Event-study pre-trend (selected leads) ===\n")
print(etable(es, stage = 2, coefstat = "se", keep = ".*-2|.*-1"))  # periods −2 and −1

# 4. Robustness check 2: Placebo reform one year earlier -------------------
df <- df %>% mutate(
  post_placebo     = ifelse(period >= 3, 1, 0),
  treat_placebo    = treated * post_placebo
)

placebo <- feols(
  y ~ treat_placebo | unit_id + period,
  data     = df,
  cluster  = ~unit_id
)

cat("\n=== Placebo DID (fake reform in period 3) ===\n")
print(coeftable(placebo)["treat_placebo", , drop = FALSE])

# 5. Optional robustness: firm-specific linear trends ----------------------
df <- df %>% mutate(period_c = period - mean(period))  # center time
trend_model <- feols(
  y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period + unit_id:period_c,
  data     = df,
  cluster  = ~unit_id
)

cat("\n=== DID with firm-specific linear trends ===\n")
print(coeftable(trend_model)["treat_x_post", , drop = FALSE])
```

The script:
1. Reads the panel,
2. Estimates the main DID,
3. Checks parallel-trend violations with an event-study (looking at leads −2, −1),
4. Runs a placebo DID (pretending the reform happened in period 3),
5. Adds firm-specific linear trends as an additional robustness check.

The `print()` calls isolate and display the point estimate and clustered s.e. for every specification so that the researcher can immediately judge magnitude and precision.

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Positive. Large firms received a bigger cut, so their marginal cost of capital fell more, leading to higher investment growth relative to small firms.

Magnitude: Roughly 0.05 – 0.10 log points (≈ 5–10 % higher investment). Economically meaningful yet plausible given typical elasticity estimates.

Robustness expectations:
• Event-study leads (−2, −1) should be statistically indistinguishable from zero → supports parallel trends.  
• Placebo coefficient should also be insignificant and near zero.  
• Including firm-specific trends should not materially change the main DID coefficient, underscoring result stability.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID with heterogeneous effects — triple-diff or interaction terms for size groups
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Large firms increase investment more than small firms post tax cut
_ground_truth.main_effect: 28% higher investment growth for large firms
